### Problem: Jump game II {#sec-od-p4-jump2}

::: {.p-statement}
From index $i$ you may jump to any index in $(i, i+\texttt{nums}[i]]$, staying inside the array. Return the minimum number of jumps from index 0 to index $n-1$. The tests guarantee that the last index is reachable. Here $1 \le n \le 10^4$ and $0 \le \texttt{nums}[i] \le 1000$.

Source: [LC 45 · Jump Game II](https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-ii/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Always jump as far as you can" takes 3 jumps on `[2,3,1,1,4]` ($0 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4$) and gets stuck on `[2,3,0,1,4]`. A long jump can land on a dead cell. What matters is the farthest index the **next** jump can reach, and that is exactly the end of the next BFS layer.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $dp[j]$ = fewest jumps from 0 to $j$, or $+\infty$ if $j$ is unreachable.
- **Transition.** Push: every reachable $i$ offers $dp[i]+1$ to each landing index.
- **Base.** $dp[0] = 0$. **Answer.** $dp[n-1]$. **Order.** Increasing $i$, because every jump goes right.
- **Layers.** The $O(n)$ scan below replaces the table once $dp$ is known to be non-decreasing.
:::

::: {#fig-od-jump2}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
dp = [10**9] * len(nums)
dp[0] = 0
for i in range(len(nums)):
    for j in range(i + 1, min(len(nums), i + nums[i] + 1)):
        dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1)
assert dp == [0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, nums, label="nums")
    V.array(ax, p, dp, 0, -1.7, label="dp", colors={0: "amber", 1: "indigo", 2: "indigo", 3: "green", 4: "green"})
V.show(draw)
```

`[2,3,1,1,4]`. The values $0,1,1,2,2$ never decrease, so each distance is a contiguous block. The last index sits in block 2.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why layers equal the min-jump DP"}
**Lemma.** If index $j$ is reachable and $i < j$, then $i$ is reachable and $dp[i] \le dp[j]$.

Take an optimal route $0 = p_0 < p_1 < \cdots < p_k = j$. Some jump flies over $i$: $p_t \le i < p_{t+1}$. That jump was legal, so $p_t + \texttt{nums}[p_t] \ge p_{t+1} > i$. The moves from $p_t$ are the whole range up to that landing, so $i$ itself is a legal landing (or $p_t = i$ already). Either way $dp[i] \le t+1 \le k = dp[j]$.

So $\{j : dp[j] \le d\}$ is a prefix $[0, R_d]$, and

$$
R_{d+1} = \min\big(n-1,\ \max_{i \le R_d}(i + \texttt{nums}[i])\big).
$$

The scan keeps `layerEnd` $= R_d$ and `farthest` $= \max_{i \le \text{current}}(i+\texttt{nums}[i])$. When $i$ arrives at `layerEnd`, `farthest` is exactly that maximum, one jump is counted, and the next layer ends there. The number of layers until one contains $n-1$ is $dp[n-1]$.

The range is the whole proof. If a cell could jump only **exactly** `nums[i]` steps, it could fly over $i$ without being allowed to stop there, the lemma would fail, and the queue would be a real BFS again. The loop stops at $i+1 < n$: the last index never jumps. Closing a layer when $i$ is already $n-1$ adds one jump too many.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
`f(i)` is the fewest jumps from `i` to the last index. Try every landing cell and add 1. `f(n-1) = 0`. If every cell can reach every later cell the tree has $2^{n-1}$ nodes. On the sample it returns 2, after re-expanding the same suffixes.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("jump2", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
INF = 10**9

def jump_rec(a):
    n = len(a)

    def f(i):
        if i == n - 1:
            return 0
        best = INF
        for j in range(i + 1, min(n, i + a[i] + 1)):
            best = min(best, 1 + f(j))
        return best

    return f(0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int jumpRec(int i, const vector<int>& a) {
    const int INF = 1e9;
    int n = (int)a.size();
    if (i == n - 1) return 0;
    int best = INF;
    for (int j = i + 1; j <= min(n - 1, i + a[i]); ++j) best = min(best, 1 + jumpRec(j, a));
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
There are only `n` questions `f(0)` … `f(n-1)`. Cache each answer the first time it returns. The loop over landing cells is unchanged.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("jump2", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def jump_memo(a):
    n = len(a)
    memo = [-1] * n

    def f(i):
        if i == n - 1:
            return 0
        if memo[i] < 0:
            best = INF
            for j in range(i + 1, min(n, i + a[i] + 1)):
                best = min(best, 1 + f(j))
            memo[i] = best
        return memo[i]

    return f(0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int jumpMemo(int i, const vector<int>& a, vector<int>& memo) {
    const int INF = 1e9;
    int n = (int)a.size();
    if (i == n - 1) return 0;
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    int best = INF;
    for (int j = i + 1; j <= min(n - 1, i + a[i]); ++j) best = min(best, 1 + jumpMemo(j, a, memo));
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Table

::: {.form-next}
Switch to prefixes: `dp[j]` is the fewest jumps from 0 to `j`. When the loop reaches `i`, every jump into `i` has already been pushed, so `dp[i]` is final and `i` may push `dp[i] + 1`. Skip a cell that is still $+\infty$. The pull form, scanning every `i < j`, fills the same table in $O(n^2)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("jump2", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def jump_table(a):
    n = len(a)
    dp = [INF] * n
    dp[0] = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if dp[i] >= INF:
            continue
        for j in range(i + 1, min(n, i + a[i] + 1)):
            dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1)
    return dp[-1]
```

##### C++

```cpp
int jumpTable(const vector<int>& a) {
    const int INF = 1e9;
    int n = (int)a.size();
    vector<int> dp(n, INF);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (dp[i] >= INF) continue;
        for (int j = i + 1; j <= min(n - 1, i + a[i]); ++j) dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i] + 1);
    }
    return dp[n - 1];
}
```
:::

#### Layers

::: {.form-next}
`farthest` is the best reach seen in the current layer. When `i` equals `layerEnd`, that layer has been scanned, including index `i` itself, so one jump is counted and the next layer ends at `farthest`. The last index is not scanned: once it lies inside the layer, the remaining jumps are already counted. On `[2,3,1,1,4]` the layer ends are 2 and then 4, which is two jumps.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("jump2", "bfs")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def jump_layers(a):
    n = len(a)
    jumps = layer_end = farthest = 0
    for i in range(n - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + a[i])
        if i == layer_end:
            jumps += 1
            layer_end = farthest
    return jumps

assert jump_layers([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]) == 2
assert jump_layers([2, 3, 0, 1, 4]) == 2
assert jump_layers([0]) == 0
assert jump_layers([2, 1, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1]) == 4
random.seed(1)
for _ in range(60):
    sample = [random.randint(1, 4) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    assert jump_rec(sample) == jump_memo(sample) == jump_table(sample) == jump_layers(sample)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int jumpLayers(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size(), jumps = 0, layerEnd = 0, farthest = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i + 1 < n; ++i) {
        farthest = max(farthest, i + a[i]);
        if (i == layerEnd) {
            jumps++;
            layerEnd = farthest;
        }
    }
    return jumps;
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** up to $\Theta(2^n)$. **Memo** and the **push table** $O(n \cdot \max \texttt{nums})$, which is about $10^7$ on the limits. **Layers** $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$ (`[0]`) is already finished: 0 jumps. A loop that runs to `i < n` returns 1.
- `[1,1]` is 1. The extra-jump bug returns 2.
- If the end were not guaranteed, `farthest <= i` at a layer boundary means the next layer is empty: return $-1$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Looping while `i < n`. When `i` lands on a `layerEnd` that is already $n-1$, one useless jump is counted. On the sample that returns 3; on `[0]` it returns 1.
- Closing the layer before reading `nums[i]`. Index `i = layerEnd` belongs to the current layer. At `i = 0` this freezes `layerEnd` at 0.
- Reusing the layer scan when a jump must have an exact length, or when jumps go left. The intervals came from the lemma, and the lemma used the range.
:::

**Variants.** [LC 55 · Jump Game](https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game/){difficulty="Medium"} only asks whether the last index is reachable: one farthest-reach integer, since the reachable cells are a prefix. [LC 1024 · Video Stitching](https://leetcode.com/problems/video-stitching/){difficulty="Medium"} turns each start time into a farthest end and runs the same layers, returning $-1$ when a layer stops growing. [LC 1345 · Jump Game IV](https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-iv/){difficulty="Hard"} jumps to equal values as well as neighbours, so the layers need a real queue.
